questions.text: If the BFP takes NO ACTION within the required period under Section 309.4, what may the Building Official do?

options.text: Deny the CO application and require the owner to re-apply after obtaining the FSIC
Issue the CO conditionally without waiting for the FSIC
Refer the matter to the Secretary of DPWH for resolution
Cancel the BFP endorsement and process the CO without fire safety review

questions.rationale: This is the highest-yield FSIC detail on the ALE. Option A (deny) would allow BFP inaction to indefinitely block occupancy — which the conditional CO provision explicitly prevents. Option B captures the correct mechanism. Option D misreads the provision as eliminating fire safety review entirely, when it only defers it.

questions.text: In PD 1096, how many Occupancy Groups (A through J) are there, and how are they subdivided?

options.text: 8 groups (A–H), subdivided into 20 Divisions
10 groups (A–J), subdivided into 25 Divisions
9 groups (A–I), subdivided into 30 Divisions
10 groups (A–J), subdivided into 15 Divisions

questions.rationale: The 10-group system with 25 divisions allows the code to match structural, fire, and egress requirements to the specific hazard level and occupant vulnerability of each building type.

questions.text: Under PD 1096, what are the divisions of Group H (Assembly Other Than Group I)?

options.text: H-1: with stage (<1,000); H-2: without stage (≥300); H-3: without stage (<300)
H-1: with stage (≥1,000); H-2: without stage (≥300); H-3: without stage (<300)
H-1: without stage (≥500); H-2: with stage (any number); H-3: outdoor venues
H-1: theaters only; H-2: restaurants; H-3: all other assembly

questions.rationale: The three criteria (stage presence, occupant load threshold of 300, and the ≥1,000 threshold for Group I) create the classification hierarchy. Stage + <1,000 → H-1. No stage + ≥300 → H-2. No stage + <300 → H-3.

questions.text: In PD 1096, what is the direction of the Construction Type sclea from Type I to Type V?

options.text: Type I = most fire-resistive; Type V = least fire-resistive, applicable to high-rise buildings
Type I = least fire-resistive (wood construction); Type V = most fire-resistive (fire-resistive construction)
Type I = masonry construction; Type V = steel construction, with specific fireproofing requirements
Type I and Type V are equivalent — they differ only in height permitted, not in fire resistance

questions.rationale: This reversal from the US IBC convention is one of the most critical exam traps. Students who import IBC mnemonics into PD 1096 answers will consistently fail questions about construction types.

questions.text: Which of the following Occupancy Groups in PD 1096 does NOT exist?

options.text: Group D (Institutional)
Group F (Industrial)
Group M (Mercantile)
Group J (Accessory)

questions.rationale: This is the US IBC vs PD 1096 trap: Group M is a US IBC classification. PD 1096 uses Group E for mercantile uses. Students familiar with US codes often answer this incorrectly.

questions.text: What is the PD 1096 occupancy classification for an aircraft hangar used for repairs?

options.text: Group E, Div. 3
Group G, Div. 5
Group F, Div. 2
Group H, Div. 4

questions.rationale: Group G covers storage and hazardous uses. The repair activity elevates this from mere storage (G Div. 1-3) or open parking (E Div. 3) to G Div. 5 for aircraft repair facilities.

questions.text: What is the PD 1096 occupancy classification for a gasoline filling station?

options.text: Group E, Div. 1
Group F, Div. 1
Group G, Div. 1
Group H, Div. 2

questions.rationale: Group F = industrial (ice plants, cold storage, factories using non-highly flammable materials). Group G = storage and hazardous (flammable materials, spray painting). Gas stations are business/mercantile under Group E despite handling flammable products — because the sales/storage is incidental to the mercantile use and the code specifically places them in E-1.

questions.text: An architect proposes a stage with a fly gallery in a building classified as Group H, Division 1. Per PD 1096, Rule XII and Rule VII, which occupancy classification applies to motion picture projection rooms within this theater?

options.text: They are classified as Group H, Division 1, the same as the theater, with no additional requirements
They are classified as ancillary to Group H, Division 1, with their own 1-hour fire-resistive construction requirement
They are classified as Group B (Business) ancillary spaces, requiring separate egress
They are exempt from occupancy classification since they are mechanical spaces, provided they meet ventilation standards

questions.rationale: Group H, Division 1 covers theaters with stage, fly gallery, and fixed seating — the most regulated assembly occupancy. The projection room is a high-hazard ancillary space (combustible film stock, electric arc equipment) but its specific requirements are contained in Section 1214 rather than the general occupancy classification rules.

questions.text: Per PD 1096, Rule XII, Section 1204, what is the maximum aggregate width of all openings in a 3-hour occupancy separation wall, expressed as a percentage of the wall's length?

options.text: 10% of wall length
20% of wall length
25% of wall length
33% of wall length

questions.rationale: The 25% limit allows meaningful penetrations (doors, windows, service openings) while ensuring the wall retains sufficient length of intact fire barrier. For a 20.00 m wall, this permits up to 5.00 m of aggregate opening width — which could be, for example, two 2.50 m door openings, provided each individual opening also stays within the 10.00 m² single-opening cap.

questions.text: According to Table XII.1 of PD 1096, what is the unit area per occupant for an auditorium, and for a warehouse?

options.text: Auditorium: 0.65 sq.m/person; Warehouse: 28.00 sq.m/person
Auditorium: 1.40 sq.m/person; Warehouse: 28.00 sq.m/person
Auditorium: 0.65 sq.m/person; Warehouse: 18.60 sq.m/person
Auditorium: 1.80 sq.m/person; Warehouse: 46.50 sq.m/person

questions.rationale: Table XII.1 specifies 0.65 sq.m/person for auditoriums (Assembly Group C) and 28.00 sq.m/person for warehouses (Industrial/Storage Group G, I). The small unit area for auditoriums reflects high-density occupancy, while the large unit area for warehouses reflects low-density storage use.

questions.text: Per PD 1096, Rule IX, Sec. 905, which buildings are required to have rat-proofing?

options.text: Only buildings above 3 storeys, as they are more susceptible to rodent infestation due to height
All buildings with hollow and/or wood construction
Only food-related establishments, which are at higher risk of contamination
Only buildings in rural areas, where rodent populations are typically higher

questions.rationale: Per Rule IX, Sec. 905, all buildings with hollow and/or wood construction shall be provided with rat-proofing. This includes concrete hollow block (CHB) buildings where open joints and cavities can become rat highways. The trigger is construction type, not occupancy classification or building size.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Chapter 7, Sec. 701, how many Occupancy Groups exist and into how many Divisions are they subdivided?

options.text: 10 groups (A through J), subdivided into 25 Divisions
8 groups (A through H), subdivided into 20 Divisions
9 groups (A through I), subdivided into 30 Divisions
10 groups (A through J), subdivided into 15 Divisions

questions.rationale: PD 1096 Sec. 701 establishes 10 Occupancy Groups (A through J) subdivided into 25 Divisions. Each group reflects a distinct profile of fire risk, occupant vulnerability, and evacuation need. The 10-group system allows the Code to match structural, fire, and egress requirements to the specific hazard level of each building type.
questions.explanation: The groups range from Group A (Residential Dwellings) through Group J (Accessory). Knowing the total count (10 groups, 25 divisions) is a baseline fact directly tested on the LEA.

questions.text: A convent houses 12 nuns on a non-leasing basis. Under PD 1096 Rule VII, Sec. 701, what is the correct occupancy classification?

options.text: Group A, Div. 1 — single-family and community residential uses
Group A, Div. 2 — residential for non-leasing occupants not exceeding 10 persons
Group B — residentials, hotels, and apartments for more than 10 persons
Group D, Div. 3 — nursing homes and similar institutional occupancies

questions.rationale: Group A Div. 2 covers convents and monasteries for non-leasing occupants not exceeding 10 persons. Once such a building accommodates more than 10 persons it becomes Group B (Residentials, Hotels and Apartments). With 12 nuns the 10-person threshold is exceeded, so the correct classification is Group B.
questions.explanation: The 10-person cutoff is one of the most frequently tested distinctions on the LEA. Group A Div. 2 → Group B is triggered the moment the non-leasing residential population exceeds 10, regardless of building type.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Sec. 703, what is the general rule for a building containing two or more occupancies?

options.text: The dominant occupancy by floor area governs the entire building classification
The building shall comply with requirements for the most restrictive occupancy involved
Each portion shall always be designed under its own occupancy requirements
Mixed-occupancy buildings are prohibited and must be separated into individual structures

questions.rationale: Sec. 703 general rule: a building with two or more occupancies shall comply with the requirements for the most restrictive occupancy involved, unless otherwise provided by the Code. This conservative approach ensures the most hazardous use governs the safety provisions for the entire structure.
questions.explanation: Two exceptions exist under Sec. 703: (a) one-storey buildings may treat each portion under its own occupancy; (b) accessory uses occupying not more than 10% of any storey may allow the major occupancy to govern.

questions.text: An assembly building has a raised stage and an occupant load of 1,200 persons. Under PD 1096 Rule VII, Sec. 701, what is the correct occupancy group?

options.text: Group H, Div. 1 — assembly with a stage, occupant load less than 1,000
Group H, Div. 2 — assembly without a stage, occupant load 300 or more
Group I — assembly with a stage AND occupant load of 1,000 or more
Group H, Div. 4 — stadia, reviewing stands, and amusement park structures

questions.rationale: Group I requires both conditions simultaneously: a stage AND an occupant load of 1,000 or more. This building has both — a raised stage and 1,200 occupants — satisfying both thresholds and qualifying as Group I. A building with a stage but fewer than 1,000 occupants falls into Group H Div. 1, not Group I.
questions.explanation: The dual condition (stage AND occupant load ≥ 1,000) is the most common Group I classification trap. Missing either condition drops the classification to the appropriate Group H division.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Sec. 703, an accessory chapel occupies 8% of the floor area of a one-storey shopping mall. Which provision governs?

options.text: The entire mall must comply with the most restrictive occupancy — religious assembly requirements, regardless of the chapel's size
The major occupancy (mall / Group E) may govern because the chapel occupies 8%, which is within the 10% accessory use threshold
The chapel must be separated and independently classified regardless of its area, ensuring compliance with all relevant codes
Mixed occupancy is prohibited in one-storey commercial buildings under Sec. 703, making the current setup non-compliant

questions.rationale: Sec. 703 Exception (b): where accessory uses occupy not more than 10% of the floor area of any storey and remain within the basic allowable area, the major occupancy may govern the classification. At 8% the chapel qualifies as a minor accessory use, so Group E (the mall's primary occupancy) governs the entire building without requiring the mall to comply with the more restrictive religious assembly standards.
questions.explanation: The 10% accessory-use exception prevents over-regulation of buildings that contain small subordinate uses. A small clinic, chapel, or daycare inside a mall need not reclassify the entire mall to institutional or religious standards if they occupy 10% or less of any storey.

questions.text: An open-air stadium without a stage accommodates 8,000 spectators. Under PD 1096 Rule VII, Sec. 701, what is the correct occupancy group?

options.text: Group I — assembly with occupant load of 1,000 or more
Group H, Div. 1 — assembly with a stage and occupant load less than 1,000
Group H, Div. 4 — stadia, reviewing stands, and amusement park structures
Group H, Div. 2 — assembly without a stage, occupant load 300 or more

questions.rationale: Group H Div. 4 covers stadia, reviewing stands, and amusement park structures not classified in Group I or H Div. 1–3. Group I requires a stage — this stadium has no stage, so it cannot be Group I regardless of its 8,000-person occupant load. Group H Div. 4 is the correct catch-all for large outdoor assembly structures without stages.
questions.explanation: The absence of a stage disqualifies any assembly facility from Group I, no matter how large the crowd. Group H Div. 4 is specifically written for sports venues and outdoor spectator facilities.

questions.text: What is the PD 1096 occupancy classification for a gasoline filling station, and why does it not fall under Group G (Storage and Hazardous)?

options.text: Group G, Div. 1 — because filling stations store hazardous flammable materials
Group F — because petroleum products are incombustible under the Code's definition
Group E, Div. 1 — the Code specifically places filling stations in Business and Mercantile
Group H, Div. 4 — because filling stations serve large numbers of the public

questions.rationale: PD 1096 Rule VII, Sec. 701 specifically lists gasoline filling and service stations under Group E (Business and Mercantile), Div. 1. Group E Div. 1 also covers storage garages and boat-storage structures where only limited maintenance is done without open flame or highly flammable liquids. The Code places filling stations in the mercantile/business category, distinguishing them from Group G which covers bulk flammable storage and industrial hazardous operations.
questions.explanation: This is a counterintuitive placement that frequently trips candidates. Even though filling stations handle flammable fuel, the Code classifies the retail sleas and service function — not the incidental fuel storage — as the principal use, placing them in Group E Div. 1.

questions.text: What is the PD 1096 occupancy classification for Group D, Div. 2, and what is the minimum number of persons that triggers it?

options.text: Mental hospitals, jails, and reformatories where liberty is restrained — more than 5 persons
Nursing homes for ambulatory patients and homes for kindergarten-age children — more than 5 persons
Hospitals and facilities with non-ambulatory patients under full medical care — more than 5 persons
Nurseries for full-time care of children under kindergarten age — more than 6 persons

questions.rationale: Group D Div. 2 covers nurseries for full-time care of children under kindergarten age, and hospitals and similar facilities with non-ambulatory patients, each accommodating more than 5 persons. The defining characteristics are: occupants under full care, non-ambulatory status, and a count of more than 5. Div. 1 covers liberty-restrained facilities (jails, mental hospitals). Div. 3 covers ambulatory nursing homes for older children (kindergarten age or over) with more than 5 occupants.
questions.explanation: The three D-division distinctions hinge on: (D1) liberty restrained; (D2) non-ambulatory or under-kindergarten care, more than 5 persons; (D3) ambulatory patients or kindergarten-age-and-over children, more than 5 occupants. Non-ambulatory status is the D2 trigger.
